title: Off Broadway Review: GIRLS CHANCE MUSIC - Bored and Confused?

Girls, Chance, Music was written by Eisa Davis, a playwright, musician, and actress who was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for her play Bull Rusher. She's also collaborated with Lin-Manuel Miranda on the Warriors concept album. This play is deeply personal. Davis grew up in San Francisco's East Bay, and spent eight summers at the Young Musicians Program, a music education initiative for low-income youth that has since become the Young Musicians Choral Orchestra. That program is essentially the setting for this play. So, she's writing about something that she knows very well. This show was commissioned back in 2018 by American Conservatory Theatre in San Francisco, one of the very first commissions made by ACT's artistic director, Pam MacKinnon, who also directs this production. MacKinnon is a Tony Award winner, by the way, and this is actually the last show she'll direct at direct as ACT's artistic director before stepping down. The world premiere ran at ACT's Strand Theater in San Francisco earlier this spring and now it has moved to the Vineyard Theater here in New York for its off-Broadway debut. It's running through June 21st. So, what is "Girl's Chance Music" about? The official description puts it this way: "During an unforgettable summer at a girls music program in Berkeley, California, 14 teenagers school each other in identity and intimacy, forging connections through passionate explorations of sound." "As the world around them thrums with disaster, their relationships crack under the weight of the unexpected and demand that they improvise new ways to being themselves." That's the official version. Here's my version. It's going to be longer. So, basically, we are following four girls. I put them in their early to mid-teens who are attending a competitive summer music program. This is a program for talented kids from families who are underserved or not super wealthy. There's Fax, an ambitious operatically trained vocalist who is laser-focused and hardworking, but can come across as intense and controlling. There's Margot, the drummer who is guarded and reserved and who believes that improvisation is the highest form of musical expression. And then there's Ryle, the pianist, who is astonishingly talented when she's sober, which is not always. And then rounding this out, we've got Clementine, a woodwind and multi-instrumentalist, who is sunny and observational and kind of floats through the emotional storms of the other three. The show really focuses on three of them: Margot, Fax, and Ryle. Margot is wrestling with suicidal thoughts. Fax is dealing with an eating disorder. And Ryle really just loves to smoke pot. Each of them is struggling. Margot is also a lesbian who develops feelings for Facts and Facts for her part just wants to collaborate with the best musician available, which happens to be Margo. There's a central creative conflict between the two of them. Margo is all about improvisation while Facts likes to do things exactly as written. Through the course of the play, Facts begins to open herself up to something looser, something more spontaneous, and develops its relationship with Margo along the way. The play also touches on and this is where it starts to get a lot eating disorders, suicide, drug use, teenage sexuality, homelessness, sperm donors, parental relationships, earthquakes. It's covering a lot of ground and like that ground in California, it can be a bit shaky. See what I did there? All right, let me talk about where the show works and where it doesn't, for me at least. Let's start with the lighting because I thought the lighting was genuinely beautiful. The opening of the show before the play even begins has these strips of light falling on each instrument on stage. It felt almost like heavenly, like some angelic force was shining down on these instruments in these beautifully wood-paneled practice rooms. It was really a lovely image. And then about halfway through the play, there's this improvisational jam session where the lights on the practice room set pieces shift into all these gorgeous colors. Visually, it was the highlight of the show for me. And the jam session itself was also the most fun I had watching this play. You can feel the energy in the room shift. Now, whether this jam session is fully improvised or a written piece designed to feel like improvisation, I think it's the latter, but either way, I feel like it works. That's when the show really felt like it was firing on all cylinders. And I have to call out the actor playing Margo, Naomi Lotta. They were the standout for me. There's an androgyny and a masculine energy to the way they played this character that I found completely fascinating. And everything they said, I believed. They have an effortlessness about them and it felt completely real. I'll also say this, the ideas in this play are genuinely interesting. The tension between improvisation and following what's on the page, the question of what it costs to become an extraordinary musician, the way music allows these girls to communicate things that they can't say in words, that's rich, compelling material. So, what didn't work for me? Here is my main issue with the show and I don't think I'm alone in this. It's just trying to do too much. There are so many plot points and themes being juggled that I kept kind of losing the most important thread. We've got eating disorders, suicide, homelessness, drug and alcohol abuse, sexual identity, lesbianism, finding your sperm donor father, earthquakes. It started to feel like I was watching several different plays all at once and I kept asking myself, what is the main idea here? What are we actually building towards? And I never quite got a satisfactory answer. The show has so many things it wants to say that none of them really get the space that they deserve. Critics who caught the world premiere in San Francisco felt the same pull. The consensus was that the play has genuine emotional intelligence and authentic characters, but the first half in particular tends to meander and that some of its more thematic moments, especially around the improvisation versus structure debate, tip into didactic territory. Margot's sustained mission to convert facts to her philosophy of jazz improvisation is compelling at first, but it gets tiresome when she keeps returning to it at the expense of the bigger, more urgent things happening in these girls' lives. And that's really my core frustration. There are genuinely big things in the story that get shortchanged. We find out that one of these girls is homeless. I assume she's living on the street after a falling out with her father and that's extraordinary dramatic material, but the play doesn't really linger there. It moves on to these smaller interpersonal tensions, and I found myself wishing the show would really focus on these more earth-shattering things that are happening in these girls' lives. There's also this audience participation moment at the top of the show. So, before the show begins, the audience can stick stickers on corresponding piano notes. There's 12 of them. And then, at the beginning of the show, the actresses have to learn that sequence. But, it felt like a gimmick that didn't pay off. It happens, and it's kind of interesting for a moment, but then it's basically dropped. It comes back once or twice, but it doesn't really address this fundamental tension between improvisation and structure. And I wanted this device to actually illuminate something, and I it just it didn't. So, the pacing also compounds everything. The show runs about 100 minutes, but it felt longer, and I think that's a structural issue more than anything else, and also a directorial issue. When a play is trying to cover this much ground, and it hasn't quite figured out its spine, the audience feels adrift. Also, the timing of the scenes, there's a lot of space between things, a lot of walking around set pieces to then establish that they were in a new space. There's a real play buried here, a smart, personal one, but I think it's still searching for its shape. So, was I bored? Yeah, I was I was pretty bored during this play. The slow pacing made it feel much longer than 100 minutes, and a lot of what I was watching just felt too small. I know these are teenage girls, and I know their concerns are going to be proportionally teenage. "She shared my music with someone else. I was much more invested in the things that were going on in their home lives. And here's the thing that frustrated me the most. There are genuinely big things happening in this story that I desperately wanted to explore. I found out that this one of the girls is homeless after a fight with her father. That's huge. That's the kind of thing I want the play to dig into. What is her relationship with her father like? How did things get so bad? What does she do with that? But the show moves on and goes back to smaller interpersonal squabbles. All the most interesting plot points felt underdeveloped. Now, I should be the target audience for the show. I love music. I love the improvisation versus on the page debate. I love the idea of young people discovering what music means to them. I'm still discovering that. And when the show started, when it opened with the character contemplating suicide framed so strikingly, I was hooked. And then the narrative just started to meander and I stopped knowing where we were going and I got I got bored. Was I confused? Yes, there's a lot of plot coming at you from a lot of different directions. The location shifts constantly from the cafeteria to a park to the apartment. And the storylines keep multiplying and by the time I was keeping track of the eating disorder and the suicidal ideation and the homelessness and the sperm donor and the relationship drama, my brain was just full. I couldn't hold it all and feel it simultaneously. The show asks a lot from its audience in terms of tracking and it doesn't always give you enough to really hold on to. So, let me wrap this up. Here's where I land. Girls, Chance, Music has the bones of a really interesting play. Icy Davis is a writer with a genuine voice and a deep personal connection to this world.
